examples: Don't go acting like a senior and ordering people around.
Even if they act grown-up, they're probably anxious inside.
I answered as if I knew it all, but my answer was full of mistakes.
I'm fed up with him lecturing everyone as if he were a teacher.
Acting like a celebrity and refusing to sign autographs makes a bad impression.
fields.explain:
Placed before the verb / subject of the next action: N + ぶって + V.
“～ぶっている” emphasizes an ongoing state or a habit of putting on airs.
Carries a critical nuance; consider politeness and social relationships when using it directly.

• The te-form of ～ぶる, used to connect clauses: “acting like / pretending to be … and (then) …”.
• Implies criticism or sarcasm toward someone “playing a role”. Stronger than ～ふりをして in its critical nuance.
• Often appears in conversation, describing the other person's behavior or tone.
fields.notes:
• “知ったかぶって” comes from “知ったかぶる” (acting as if one knows when one actually doesn't); a common phrase with a mocking nuance.
• Often used with nouns for roles or status: 先生／専門家／先輩／上司／有名人／被害者 など。
• In spoken language, “～ぶってさ…” is used to open a complaint, with a casual nuance.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～ふりをして: JLPT questions often test the critical nuance of ～ぶって.
Using “～ぶって” with an i-adjective that has not been nominalized (×賢いぶって → 賢いふりをして/賢そうぶって).
Forgetting to conjugate ～ぶる for the context and tense: when describing a current state, use ～ぶっている; it is not always ～ぶって.

examples: He's always acting grown-up, but inside he's still a child.
She explains everything as if she knows it all, so it's sometimes a problem.
It's not good to look down on people with a gentlemanly air.
He acts like he's poor, yet he wears an expensive watch.
He acts like a senior and does nothing but give orders.
fields.explain:
Usually colloquial; the critical/sarcastic nuance is quite clear. Be careful in polite situations.
Progressive/connecting forms: ～ぶって（て形）and ～ぶった（past/modifier）are very common when criticizing someone's attitude.
It combines naturally with relatively few words; it often appears in fixed phrases:大人ぶる,知ったかぶる,先生ぶる, いい子ぶる, かわいこぶる.

• “～ぶる” expresses superficial behavior of “acting like / putting on airs / pretending”, usually with a critical or sarcastic nuance.
• Attaches to nouns for roles or qualities: 大人ぶる（act grown-up）, 先生ぶる（act like a teacher）, 知ったかぶる（act like a know-it-all）.
• Unlike ～がる (showing a real feeling) and ～げ (seeming), ～ぶる implies “trying to look like”, with a strong sense of fakeness.
fields.notes:
• “知ったかぶる” is a shortened form of “知ったかぶりをする”. The noun form “～ぶり” here (different from the ～ぶり in 仕事ぶり) means “the habit of putting on airs”.
• In ads and headlines, it is sometimes used for wordplay: プロぶった素人（an amateur acting like a pro）.
• For a stronger degree, ～気取り (きどり) can be used: 貴族気取り（putting on airs like an aristocrat）, with a highly contemptuous nuance.
mistakes: Attaching it to the dictionary form of an i-adjective: 高いぶる（incorrect）→ use a noun/語幹: 上品ぶる, プロぶる.
Using it in formal writing is rude: avoid direct criticism of customers or business partners.
Confusing it with ～がる: ～ぶる means “pretend / act like”, not “feel”.

examples: If nobody will help me, I'll just do it myself.
If I fail, I'll simply take the exam again.
I only answered because I was asked.
I only did what was natural.
If I do my best and it still doesn't work, I'll just give up.
fields.explain:
Formal; often seen in written language and serious speeches. It is also used in spoken language, but sounds calm and decisive.
Vた + までだ is humble, downplaying one's own contribution to be polite.
Vる + までだ usually comes with a context of “no other way / no one to help / no other choice”.

• Vる + までだ: said when there is no better option, with a nuance of “I'll have to”. It can also express resolve or self-reassurance.
• Vた + までだ: downplays the merit or significance of one's own action: “I only did what was natural”. Often used when praised or misunderstood.
• “～までのことだ” is equivalent, more polite/softer than “～までだ”.
fields.notes:
• “まで” originally means “up to / as far as”; in this pattern it shifts to “to the point where the only option is …”.
• Often used with condition/supposition structures: もし～なら／万一～なら … ～までだ.
• Vた + までだ is often used when praised, to avoid boasting: お役に立てて何よりです。したまでです。
mistakes: Confusing Vた + までだ (I only … ) with Vる + までだ (I'll have to …): their functions are different.
Using the humble meaning “したまでだ” with someone else as the subject is pragmatically wrong; it is usually the speaker talking about themselves.
Mixing it up with ～しかない: both are grammatically correct, but the JLPT tests the formal/resolute nuance of ～までだ.

rows: Have to / the only option is
Vる + しかない／ほかない

examples: I went to see the section chief, partly to say hello as well.
I went around the new factory, also as a tour of inspection.
I'm going on a business trip to Hokkaido that will double as sightseeing.
I watch Japanese dramas partly for study as well.
I will share the results by email, which will also serve as my report.
Allow me to greet you, and to exchange business cards at the same time.
fields.explain:
Use it when there are two purposes at the same time that are both reasonable and do not conflict.
Works well with verbs of motion:行く・伺う・訪問する・回る・参加する; and with verbs of sending/exchanging:送る・連絡する。
More formal than ～ついでに; more neutral than ～がてら (relaxed) and less formal than ～かたがた.
In business, it helps you speak politely and indirectly:挨拶も兼ねて伺いました (instead of “I came just to say hello”).

• Expresses “also serving as, at the same time as / in order to” – doing one thing for purpose A while also achieving purpose B.
• Focus: intentionally combining purposes. Slightly more formal than ～ついでに, friendlier than ～かたがた.
• The preceding noun is usually the secondary/accompanying purpose: 挨拶, 見学, 視察, 連絡, 報告, 観光, 勉強, PR…
• Often used in business and social courtesy contexts, politely; also used in everyday life.
• Not used with immoral or reluctant actions.
fields.notes:
• Nouns that express an “activity / purpose” sound more natural: 見学・挨拶・報告・観光・勉強・応援.
• It does not combine directly with a clause; if needed, nominalize it: 安全確認も兼ねて点検する.
• A polite pattern in business emails: 「ご挨拶も兼ねてご連絡申し上げます」。
mistakes: Mixing it up with ～ついでに: the JLPT often asks about nuance; ～も兼ねて is more formal and emphasizes “serving a double purpose”.
Using it directly with an adjective or verb is incorrect: it needs a noun (or a nominalization).
Choosing an unnatural noun: avoid abstract nouns that are not activities (例: 幸せも兼ねて ×).

examples: Helped by the good weather, the number of visitors reached a record high.
Combined with his efforts, the project was a success.
Combined with the trend of a weak yen, exporters' profits are growing.
Combined with how quickly it spread on social media, it became a hot topic in no time.
Combined with its good location, this shop is always crowded.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to emphasize a “combination of causes” rather than attributing the result to a single factor.
Often used in narration and reports; a more formal style than everyday conversation.
Suitable for both positive and negative results:人手不足も相まって納期が遅れた。

• “Working together with, combined with” – several factors act at the same time to produce a stronger result.
• An objective tone explaining combined causes; often seen in reports and news.
• Position: between the cause part and the result part; mainly about good/bad results caused by several factors.
• The factor before ～も相まって is usually an additional factor, not the only cause.
fields.notes:
• Often used for social/economic/market phenomena: 物価高、円安、好景気、不況…
• Avoid repeating ～も相まって several times in one sentence; list them as Aに、Bも相まって…
• The subject is usually the result/situation, not the agent of an action.
mistakes: Using it for a single cause → not appropriate; use ～だけに or ～ので.
Using it in very casual spoken language → sounds stiff; consider ～もあって.
Confusing it with ～に加えて: the JLPT tests the nuance of “working together” vs. “in addition”.

examples: The parents are bad, and so is the child.
The staff are bad, and the customers are just as bad.
The boss is bad, and the subordinates are no better.
The rain is bad, and so is the wind; today is the worst.
The school is bad, and so are the parents, aren't they?
The response is bad, and so is the explanation. I can't accept this.
fields.explain:
Often used in spoken language, on social media, and in sensational headlines, with a sarcastic nuance.
The two nouns are usually two related or corresponding “sides” (parent–child, shop–customer, team–fans).
Not appropriate in extremely formal contexts or when emotional neutrality is needed.
Often accompanied by evaluative words: ひどい,最低, いい加減,雑, ずさん …
Can stand alone as a comment:親も親なら、子も子だ。

• Meaning: “A is just like A, and B is just like B” → emphasizes that both sides have problems / are worth remarking on, usually with a nuance of criticism, sarcasm or complaint.
• Speaker's emotion: a strongly subjective evaluation; often used when disappointed, frustrated, or “too fed up to say more”.
• Pragmatics: usually used with nouns referring to people, organizations or targets of the same kind, compared in parallel: 親−子, 店−客, 上司−部下, 学校−生徒.
• Syntax: the N before and after も is usually the same noun repeated (emphasizing “that's just how … is”). The second clause uses だ/だった to conclude the evaluation.
• Tense: both present and past are possible; future is rare. The polite form です can be used, but the sarcastic nuance remains.
fields.notes:
• This structure usually has parallel syllables, creating a sarcastic “rhythm”; so the noun is repeated exactly.
• The order of the two clauses can be reversed depending on which side you want to emphasize.
• To soften it, you can add ね or なあ at the end of the sentence, or use です/ます.
mistakes: Using an adjective/verb instead of a repeated noun: incorrect. The standard pattern is a noun repeated before も.
Using it in formal documents such as official reports: inappropriate because of its strong emotional nuance.
Misunderstanding it as praising both: it almost always has a negative/complaining meaning.
Forgetting tense/negation: the second clause needs to end with だ/です/だった according to the appropriate tense.

fields.meaning: Not sure whether to… or not…
fields.connection: V volitional form + か + Vる + まいか
examples: I couldn't decide whether to go or not until the last minute.
I thought many times about whether or not to tell him the truth.
I agonized over whether to take part or not until the deadline.
I'm talking with my family about whether or not to study abroad.
They discussed whether or not to stay here.
fields.explain:
Used when describing a process of deliberation; usually not used for commands or requests.
Can be followed by a nominalization: ～ようか～まいか＋迷い／悩み.
More formal in style than ～かどうか (neutral).

- Expresses hesitation: “whether to do it or not…”. Usually expresses an inner monologue, weighing up a decision.
- The subject is usually the speaker (first person) or a group deliberating; often accompanied by 迷う／悩む／決めかねる／考える.
- Has a formal/slightly literary nuance; “まい” is the classical negative volitional form.
fields.notes:
• Standard: Vる＋まい; with 一段 verbs, Vまい is sometimes seen in spoken language, but exams prefer Vるまい.
• With する: both するまい/すまい are correct; すまい is more natural.
• With 来る: 来るまい／来まい (来まい leans toward written language).
mistakes: Choosing ～ようが～るまいが (regardless) by mistake when the context is “hesitating”.
Using it with adjectives/nouns: ×「高いようか高くあるまいか」 (only used with verbs).
Wrong form: ×「食べまいか食べようか」 (the standard order is 食べようか食べるまいか).

Emphasizes “should / should not” rather than pure hesitation

Whether or not one does it, still…

fields.connection: V volitional form + が + Vる + まいが
examples: Whether it rains or not, the match will be held as scheduled.
Whether he agrees or not, we will go ahead with the plan.
Whoever comes or doesn't come, I'll do what I have to do.
Whether you succeed or not, the fact that you tried has meaning.
Whether the economy is good or bad, we will keep investing.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes resolve / a stance that does not change in the face of opposite conditions.
The second clause usually affirms a position; it is not used for questions or requests.
Formal style, used in speeches and essays.

- Expresses a firm stance: “whether one does it or not … (still) …”. The second clause shows an action/decision that is not affected.
- Formal nuance, used in speeches, arguments and declarations of resolve.
- Usually appears with a tight parallel correspondence between the two preceding clauses.
fields.notes:
• Keep the forms parallel: V-ようが ↔ V-るまいが with the same verb.
• Extending it to adjectives/nouns allows more varied expression in argumentative writing.
• Formal style; in everyday conversation it can be replaced with ～ても～なくても.
mistakes: Not keeping the same verb in both parts: ×「行こうが 来るまいが」 → correct: 「行こうが 行くまいが」.
Using it to ask a question or make a request → does not fit its declarative nuance.
Confusing it with ～ようか～るまいか in pattern-choice questions: look at the second clause; if it is “still… / continue…”, choose ～ようが～るまいが.

fields.connection: V volitional form + と + Vる + まいと
examples: Whether he comes or not, the meeting will start as scheduled.
Whether it rains or not, the match will continue.
Whether she agrees or not, the policy will not change.
Whatever people say to me, or don't say, I'll go my own way.
Whether the company supports him or not, he intends to see it through on his own.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to affirm a stance or principle: the second clause usually has a decisive meaning.
Formal; appears in speeches, written language and news reports.
The two preceding clauses should correspond, using the same verb, to create rhythm and symmetry.
Not used for invitations or direct requests.

The pattern ～ようと～るまいと expresses “whether one does (V) or not, the conclusion/judgment that follows does not change”. Equivalent to “whether … or not …”. Formal nuance, in a written/speech style.
• Emphasizes that the second clause is “unchanging” in the face of every opposing possibility (doing / not doing).
• Often talks about resolve, policies, general tendencies, or the irrelevance of the preceding condition to the result.
• The preceding clauses usually use the same verb in two forms: volitional (Vよう) and negative volitional (Vるまい).
fields.notes:
• “まい” is a negative volitional form with an archaic/written nuance; in conversation “〜ても〜なくても” is usually used.
• With 来る: 来るまい（くるまい）；with する: するまい. Avoid “来まい/すまい” in standard modern Japanese (except in a very archaic style).
• Different subjects can be inserted in the two preceding clauses, but the same subject is usually kept for coherence.
mistakes: Using different verbs in the two parts: the same verb is required (行こうと来るまいと → incorrect).
Confusing “Vないと” with “Vるまいと”: “まい” is the negative volitional, not “ない”.
Using it in everyday conversation sounds stiff; for the JLPT you need to recognize its formal nuance.
Confusing it with “〜ようにも〜れない” (expressing “even if one wants to, one cannot”), whereas this pattern means “whether one does it or not, the result that follows does not change”.
